vignette:
Leilani was nineteen when the world ended for a day. She remembers the warmth of the sun on her arms at a family wedding feast, the sweet scent of frangipani, and the rare, uncomplicated feeling of happiness. Then came the sirens. They were hurried into a packed, subterranean shelter, a concrete box crammed with terrified strangers. For the next twelve hours, the only sensory input was the shudder of bombs overhead and the thick, sour smell of sweat and fear from the bodies pressed tight against hers in the dark. That day left a mark that sixty years of a quiet, orderly life as an auditor in America could not erase. The trauma never became a story she could tell; when she tries, she finds she knows what happened but is unable to find the words to describe it. Instead, it lives in her as a collection of silent, vivid snapshots.

The memories rarely announce themselves. More often, they are summoned by the mundane. Just last week, during an audit in a stuffy, windowless conference room, the scent of a nervous client’s body odour caught her, and instantly, she was no longer a respected 75-year-old professional but a girl in a dark cellar, the photographic recall of terrified faces flashing behind her eyes. The intrusion was so powerful that for the rest of the afternoon, she was convinced the client could see the horror on her face, confirming her deep-seated belief that the trauma she carries is a visible stain on her character. A simple moment of joy, like laughing with her husband, can feel like a betrayal of that past, and the happiness evaporates, replaced by the conviction that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again. These triggers pull her back not just to the event, but to the devastating beliefs it left in its wake.

Over the decades, these beliefs have hardened into certainties. Leilani is convinced that her trauma is a visible stain, that others can see what happened to her just by looking at her. This deep-seated feeling of being exposed governs her every move. At her firm, she is known for her peculiar habit of only sitting in chairs that are flush against a wall, a position from which she can see the entire room and, more importantly, ensure no one can stand behind her. Her walk from the train station to her office is a tense, furtive exercise in constantly checking behind her, certain that someone is following, watching, and seeing the damage she carries. Because these scanning behaviours never allow her to simply walk and arrive safely without incident, her nervous system never learns that the street is safe; instead, it concludes that her vigilance is the only thing preventing an ever-present disaster. The memory of total helplessness in the shelter fuels a present-day sense of imminent threat; if she was so vulnerable then, she must be perpetually unsafe now. This core belief that her safety is an illusion means that every unfamiliar face on the street, every unexpected noise, carries a weight of potential danger.

In the quiet of her own mind, Leilani is locked in a relentless effort to control the past. After a memory intrudes, she spends hours ruminating, going over and over why the event happened to her and meticulously replaying the moments before the sirens, searching for a different choice she could have made that would have prevented it all. This mental churning does not bring peace; instead, it keeps the photographic images sharp and accessible, ensuring they are always ready to surface. The constant rehearsal of what to say before any social interaction, an attempt to appear normal, only reinforces her belief that she is a fraud and that her life, lived behind such a careful mask, is not worth living anymore. This profound sense of worthlessness seems to call up the trauma itself, as if her mind is presenting the core evidence for her despair, flooding her again with the silent, photographic images from the shelter. The rumination and the memories feed a constant, low-grade sense of threat, which in turn makes her hypervigilant, and that feeling of being hunted often triggers the memories anew.

The cycle has grown tighter with age. Her world has shrunk to the predictable routes between home and work, places where she can manage her seating and her interactions. Even there, safety is an illusion. A colleague walking too closely behind her in the hallway can bring back the images with nauseating force. In a strange, quiet rebellion against this state of constant alert, she sometimes engages in risky behaviour, taking the long way home through a poorly lit park, as if daring the world to do its worst and prove her feelings of dread right. It was after one such evening, when her husband’s frantic relief at her return was met with her flat, empty admission that she wasn’t sure her life was worth living anymore, that he made the appointment for her. Leilani sits in the therapy room now, her back firmly to the wall, not with any real hope, but with the quiet, desperate fear that the pictures in her head have finally consumed everything else.
